planting.note: Scatter seed on raked, well-drained soil in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy naturally; plants form a basal rosette the first year and send up tall bloom spikes the following spring.

directions: This Sonoran and Chihuahuan desert grassland native throws up slender spikes of vivid coral-red tubular flowers each spring, towering well above the low foliage clump and drawing hummingbirds from a distance. Give it rocky or gravelly soil with sharp drainage and resist the urge to water on a regular schedule, since soggy roots are the main cause of failure in cultivation. It is short-lived but reseeds readily in open gravel mulch, so leave a few spent spikes standing to scatter seed for the next generation. Cut back old flower stalks after seed drops to keep the basal rosette tidy through summer dormancy.

common_name: Perky Sue (Stemless Four-Nerve Daisy, Angelita Daisy)

planting.note: Sow or set out small plants in spring in gritty, lean soil; this tight evergreen mat establishes quickly and often blooms the same season it is planted.

directions: Perky Sue forms a dense, almost stemless rosette of narrow silvery-green leaves that stays attractive year-round, studded with bright yellow one-inch daisies on wiry stems from spring well into fall. It is remarkably tolerant of poor, rocky, alkaline soils and needs almost no supplemental water once established, making it a dependable edger for gravel paths, rock gardens, and xeric borders across a surprisingly wide elevation range. Deadheading spent flowers extends the bloom season, though the plant looks neat even left alone. Division of older clumps in early spring is an easy way to multiply plantings without starting from seed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring into sandy, well-drained soil; give the sprawling branches room since mature plants spread much wider than tall.

directions: Rosemary Mint is a loose, silvery-leaved desert subshrub whose fine aromatic foliage releases a minty-sage scent when brushed, with small white flowers flecked lavender appearing intermittently from spring through fall. It thrives on sandy, eroded, alkaline slopes and gypsum hills where almost nothing else survives, and in the garden it wants the same lean, fast-draining conditions with infrequent deep watering. Because it roots readily from semi-hardwood cuttings, propagating named stock is easier than growing it from seed. An occasional light shearing after bloom keeps the sprawling habit from becoming woody and open in the center.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring (or fall in mild low-desert gardens) onto disturbed, well-drained soil; this short-lived plant self-sows freely once a patch is established.

directions: Spreading Fleabane produces loose mounds of narrow leaves topped by dozens of small, cheerful daisies with white-to-pink rays and yellow centers, blooming over an unusually long stretch from spring through the summer monsoon. It is an easygoing short-lived perennial that colonizes roadside gravel, wash margins, and disturbed ground across the desert Southwest, making it a reliable filler for rock gardens and pollinator borders where it reseeds without becoming aggressive. Butterflies and small native bees visit the flowers heavily, and plants that are sheared back lightly after the first flush often rebloom. It tolerates poor soil and benefits from being left slightly crowded, which supports its sprawling habit.

planting.note: Nick or soak the hard legume seed coat before sowing in spring into gritty, well-drained soil; this low grower is better suited to rock gardens than to mass bedding.

directions: Dwarf Fairyduster is the compact, foot-tall cousin of the more familiar pink fairyduster shrub, spreading as a low mat of fine pea-family foliage topped with the same pink-and-white powderpuff blooms from spring into summer. It is notably cold-hardy for a desert legume and thrives at higher elevations in rocky, dry grassland and woodland-edge soils where many lowland desert plants would suffer frost damage. The flowers feed native bees, and the foliage is a larval host for ceraunus and marine blue butterflies, so it earns a spot in a pollinator garden even though it is less showy than its larger relatives. Light supplemental water during the hottest months keeps the mat denser without pushing excessive soft growth.

planting.note: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks ahead and set transplants out after the last frost into mineral, sharply drained soil; established clumps tolerate being tucked into rocky slopes or canyon-style borders.

directions: Crimson Sage is a compact, woody-based perennial native to grasslands and piñon-juniper canyons of the Texas/New Mexico/Arizona borderlands near the Chihuahuan Desert, producing an unusually long season of bright crimson, tubular flowers that hummingbirds seek out from spring well into fall. It needs sharp drainage and sparing water far more than rich soil, and overwatering or heavy clay will quickly rot the roots. A light trim after the first flush of bloom encourages a second round of flowers and keeps the woody base from sprawling open. In a xeriscape or rock-garden setting it pairs well with other Southwest natives that share the same lean, dry preferences.

planting.note: Sow or transplant in spring into fast-draining desert soil; this rangy subshrub needs room to reach its full width and resents competition from denser plantings.

directions: Button Brittlebush is a sandpaper-leaved, green-stemmed subshrub that fills desert washes and rocky flats with masses of petal-less, nectar-rich yellow flower heads whenever summer monsoon rain triggers a bloom flush, drawing heavy traffic from bees and butterflies. Unlike its showier relative the common brittlebush, it keeps a looser, more open silhouette that reads as texture rather than color for most of the year. It asks for nothing more than full sun, sharp drainage, and benign neglect, tolerating long dry spells and poor caliche soils without complaint. Cutting back lightly after a hard freeze removes winter-damaged tips and keeps the shrub from becoming leggy.

planting.note: Sow directly in early summer so seedlings are in place when monsoon rains arrive; this ephemeral germinates and flowers in response to summer moisture and sets seed before frost.

directions: Sawtooth Sage is a slender, upright monsoon annual that spends most of the year as dormant seed, then germinates with the first summer rains and quickly sends up small deep-purple, white-marked flowers along toothed-leaf stems. It grows in both open sunny, sandy sites and the dappled light of rocky canyon slopes across the desert Southwest, so it tolerates a range of light conditions in a garden setting. Because it completes its whole life cycle in a few warm, wet months, it works best scattered among perennial desert natives rather than grown as a stand-alone bedding plant. Letting a portion of the stand go to seed each year is the easiest way to keep it returning.
